title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Main1}
	Let $\mathcal{G}_\Gamma$ be a graph product of cyclic groups. Then:
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item If $\Gamma^{<\infty}$ is a clique, then
		$$ \beta_i^{(2)}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)=\frac{1}{\left|\mathcal{G}_{\Gamma^{<\infty}}\right|}\left(\sum_{\Omega\subset\Gamma^{<\infty}}\left(\prod_{w\in V(\Gamma^{<\infty}\setminus\Omega)}(o(w)-1)\right)\beta_i^{(2)}(A_{\Gamma\setminus\Omega})\right)\qquad\text{for all } i\geq 0.$$
		\item If $V(\Gamma^{<\infty})=\{u_1,\dots,u_n\}$ and $\operatorname{lk}(u_1)=\cdots=\operatorname{lk}(u_n)=:L$,	then
		$$
		\beta_i^{(2)}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)
		=
		\beta_i^{(2)}(A_{\Gamma_{\mathcal{U}_1}})
		+
		\left(
		n-1-\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{1}{o(u_j)}
		\right)
		\beta_{i-1}^{(2)}(A_L)
		\qquad\text{for all } i\geq 0,
		$$
		where $\Gamma_{\mathcal{U}_1}$ is the graph obtained from $\Gamma$ by deleting $u_2,\dots,u_n$.
	\end{enumerate}

Let $G$ be a finitely generated group and $\chi:G\to\mathbb{R}$ a character. If $A$ is a left $G$-module and $n\geq 1$, the \textbf{Bieri–Neumann–Strebel–Renz (BNSR) invariants} are defined by

	$$
	where $G_\chi=\{g\in G\mid\chi(g)\geq 0\}$.

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $G$ be a group admitting a finite $K(G,1)$, and let $X$ be a finite model for $K(G,1)$ having a single 0-cell. There is a bijection between the vertices of the universal cover $\widetilde{X}$ and the elements of $G$. Fix a base point $b\in\widetilde{X}^{(0)}$. Given a character $\chi:G\to\mathbb{R}$, define a function $\widetilde{\chi}:\widetilde{X}^{(0)}\to\mathbb{R}$ by $\widetilde{\chi}(g\cdot b)=\chi(g)$. For $a\in\mathbb{R}$, let $\widetilde{X_{\chi}}^{[a,\infty)}$ be the maximal subcomplex of $\widetilde{X}$ with $0$-skeleton $\{x\in\widetilde{X}^{(0)}\mid \widetilde{\chi}(x)\geq a\}$. Then, for each $d\geq 0$, the inclusion $\widetilde{X_{\chi}}^{[0,\infty)}\hookrightarrow \widetilde{X_{\chi}}^{[-d,\infty)}$ induces a map $\tau_i^d:\pi_i\bigl(\widetilde{X_{\chi}}^{[0,\infty)}\bigr)\longrightarrow \pi_i\bigl(\widetilde{X_{\chi}}^{[-d,\infty)}\bigr).$
	Define the \textbf{homotopical Sigma invariants} by
	$$\Sigma^n(G)=\Bigl\{[\chi]\in S(G)\ \Bigm|\ \exists\, d>0 \text{ such that }\tau_i^d\text{ is trivial for all } i<n \Bigr\}.$$

title: Proof
body_md:
We argue by induction on $i$. For $i=0$, the reduced zeroth Betti number equals the number of connected components minus $1$, so it suffices to count connected components. Let $r$ denote the number of connected components of $\widehat{\Gamma}$, and let $l$ denote the number of connected components of $\widehat{\Gamma}$ that intersect $\Delta$. Then the number of connected components of $\widehat{\Omega}$ is $l+(r-l)n$, while the number of connected components of $\widehat{\gamma}$ is $r-l+1$. Hence, the formula follows.
	
	Now assume $i\geq 1$. Applying the Mayer--Vietoris long exact sequence to $\widehat{\Omega}$ yields
	$$\cdots \rightarrow (n-1)\overline{\mathrm{H}}_i(\widehat{\Delta})\rightarrow n\overline{\mathrm{H}}_i(\widehat{\Gamma})\rightarrow \overline{\mathrm{H}}_i(\widehat{\Omega})\rightarrow \cdots.$$
	Similarly, applying the Mayer--Vietoris long exact sequence to $\widehat{\gamma}$ gives
	$$\cdots \rightarrow \overline{\mathrm{H}}_i(\widehat{\Delta})\rightarrow \overline{\mathrm{H}}_i(\widehat{\Gamma})\oplus \overline{\mathrm{H}}_i(\widehat{\Delta}_1)\rightarrow \overline{\mathrm{H}}_i(\widehat{\gamma})\rightarrow \cdots .$$
	Since $\widehat{\Delta}_1$ is contractible, multiplying this long exact sequence by $n-1$ we obtain
	$$\cdots \rightarrow (n-1)\overline{\mathrm{H}}_i(\widehat{\Delta})\rightarrow (n-1)\overline{\mathrm{H}}_i(\widehat{\Gamma})\rightarrow (n-1)\overline{\mathrm{H}}_i(\widehat{\gamma})\rightarrow \cdots .$$
	Adding a $\overline{\mathrm{H}}_i(\widehat{\Gamma})$ term to the middle group yields
	$$\cdots \rightarrow (n-1)\overline{\mathrm{H}}_i(\widehat{\Delta})\rightarrow n\overline{\mathrm{H}}_i(\widehat{\Gamma})\rightarrow (n-1)\overline{\mathrm{H}}_i(\widehat{\gamma})\oplus \overline{\mathrm{H}}_i(\widehat{\Gamma})\rightarrow \cdots .
	$$
	Thus, we obtain two long exact sequences in which, by the induction hypothesis, the groups in degrees $i$ and $i-1$ agree. By the Five Lemma, this induces an isomorphism in the middle groups
	$$\overline{\mathrm{H}}_i(\widehat{\Omega})\cong(n-1)\overline{\mathrm{H}}_i(\widehat{\gamma})\oplus\overline{\mathrm{H}}_i(\widehat{\Gamma}).$$
	Taking dimensions completes the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
Proceed by induction over $\left| V(\Gamma^{<\infty})\right|$. For the base case, say $\Gamma^{<\infty}=\lbrace v\rbrace$ and $o(v)=n$, let $\Delta:=\Gamma_v\ast_{\operatorname{lk}(v)}\stackrel{n}{\cdots}\ast_{\operatorname{lk}(v)}\Gamma_v$. By Proposition \ref{Endomorphism} applied to the map $\varphi:\mathcal{G}_\Gamma\to\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ defined as $\varphi(v)=v$ and $\varphi(w)=0~\forall~w\neq v$, we have $\beta_i^{(2)}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)=\frac{1}{n}\beta_i^{(2)}(A_{\Delta})$. Using Theorem \ref{BettiRAAG} and Proposition \ref{AmalgamatedGraph}:
	$$\beta_i^{(2)}(A_\Delta)=(n-1)\beta_i^{(2)}(A_\Gamma)+\beta_i^{(2)}(A_{\Gamma_v})~\forall~i\geq 0$$
	and the base case follows. For the induction step suppose that the formula holds for all graph products $\mathcal{G}_\Lambda$ such that $\left| V(\Lambda^{<\infty})\right|=r$. Assume that $\mathcal{G}_\Gamma$ satisfies $\left| V(\Gamma^{<\infty})\right|=r+1$. Take $v\in V(\Gamma^{<\infty})$ and assume that $o(v)=n$ and define $\Delta$ and $\varphi$ as before. By proposition  \ref{Endomorphism} we have that $\beta_i^{(2)}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)=\frac{1}{n}\beta_i^{(2)}(\mathcal{G}_{\Delta})$ and $\Delta$ is a graph such that $\left| V(\Delta^{<\infty})\right|=r$. Apply the induction hypothesis to $\Delta$:
	$$\beta_i^{(2)}(\mathcal{G}_\Delta)=\frac{1}{\left|\mathcal{G}_{\Delta^{<\infty}}\right|}\left(\sum_{\Omega\subset\Delta^{<\infty}}\left(\prod_{w\in V(\Delta^{<\infty}\setminus\Omega)}(o(w)-1)\right)\beta_i^{(2)}(A_{\Delta\setminus\Omega})\right)~\forall~i\geq 0$$
	Using Proposition \refeq{AmalgamatedGraph} and Theorem \ref{BettiRAAG}:
	$$\beta_i^{(2)}(A_{\Delta\setminus\Omega})=(o(v)-1)\beta_i^{(2)}(A_{\Gamma\setminus\Omega})+\beta_i^{(2)}(A_{\Gamma\setminus(\Omega\cup \lbrace v\rbrace)})~\forall~i\geq 0,\Omega\subset\Delta^{<\infty}$$
	and substituting this into the above equation the result follows.

title: Lemma
body_md:
There are
	$$
	A:=m\left(n-1-\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{1}{o(u_j)}\right)+1
	$$
	non-zero generators of the form $\prescript{j}{}{X_{i_1,\dots,i_n}}$. They are exactly the ones satisfying that $1\leq j\leq n-1$, $0\leq i_k<o(u_k)$ for each $1\leq k\leq n$, $i_j\neq0$ and $(i_{j+1},\dots,i_n)\neq(0,\dots,0)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Two generators of a graph product of cyclic groups commute if and only if they are connected in the defining graph. Hence, since $u_i$ is not connected to $u_j$ for any indices $i$ and $j$, we have $[u_{j+1}^{i_{j+1}}\cdots u_n^{i_n},u_j]=1$
	if and only if $(i_{j+1},\dots,i_n)=(0,\dots,0)$. Thus, for each $j$, the number of non-zero distinct generators $\prescript{j}{}{X_{i_1,\dots,i_n}}$ equals the number of $n$-tuples
	$(i_1,\dots,i_n)$ satisfying
	$$
	0\leq i_k<o(u_k)\ \text{ for all } 1\leq k\leq n,\quad
	i_j\neq 0,\quad
	(i_{j+1},\dots,i_n)\neq (0,\dots,0).
	$$
	The number of such $n$-tuples is
	$$o(u_1)\cdots o(u_{j-1})\bigl(o(u_j)-1\bigr)\bigl(o(u_{j+1})\cdots o(u_n)-1\bigr).	$$
	Hence, the total number of non-zero generators is
	$$\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}o(u_1)\cdots o(u_{j-1})\bigl(o(u_j)-1\bigr)\bigl(o(u_{j+1})\cdots o(u_n)-1\bigr).$$
	A straightforward calculation shows that this sum equals $A$.

title: Proof

title: Definition
body_md: Let $G$ be a torsion-free group. We say that $G$ satisfies the \textbf{Atiyah conjecture} if the Linnell ring $\mathcal{D}(G)$ is a division ring.

title: Remark
body_md: Although this is not the standard formulation of the Atiyah conjecture, a result of Linnell (see \cite{Linell}) shows that, for torsion-free groups, it is equivalent to the Atiyah conjecture over $\mathbb{Q}$.

title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Lemma
body_md:
Let $G=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_d\mid r=1\rangle$ be a torsion-free one-relator group. Then
	$$
	\beta_i^{(2)}(G)=
	\begin{cases}
		d-2, & \text{if } i=1,\\
		0, & \text{otherwise}.
	\end{cases}
	$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By a theorem of Brodskii and Howie, every torsion-free one-relator group is locally indicable (see \cite{Brodski} and \cite{Howie}). In particular, $G$ satisfies the Atiyah conjecture, and hence the Linnell division ring $\mathcal{D}(G)$ is defined.
	
	Let	$f\in\operatorname{Der}(G,\mathcal{D}(G))$ and write the relator as a reduced word $r=a_1\cdots a_n$, where $a_i\in\{x_1^{\pm1},\ldots,x_d^{\pm1}\}$.
	
	Since $r=1$ in $G$, we have $0=f(r)
	=f(a_1)+a_1f(a_2)+\cdots+a_1\cdots a_{n-1}f(a_n)$. Moreover, for every generator $x_i$ we have $f(x_i^{-1})=-x_i^{-1}f(x_i)$. Choose a generator $x_j$ which occurs in the relator $r$. The above relation therefore determines $f(x_j)$ uniquely in terms of the values	$f(x_i)$ for $i\neq j$.	Consequently, $\operatorname{Der}(G,\mathcal{D}(G))\cong \mathcal{D}(G)^{d-1}$ and $\beta_1^{(2)}(G)=d-2$.
	
	Finally, torsion-free one-relator groups have cohomological dimension at most $2$ with the presentation complex as the classifying space (cf. \cite{Putnam} Theorem 7.1). Hence, 
	$\beta_i^{(2)}(G)=0$ for all $i>2$ and $\chi(G)=2-d$. Since $G$ is infinite, $\beta_0^{(2)}(G)=0$, and therefore $\beta_2^{(2)}(G)=\beta_1^{(2)}(G)+\chi(G)=0$.

label: Derivation Lemma
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $uv=vu$ then $f(uv)=f(vu)\Rightarrow f(u)+uf(v)=f(v)+vf(u)\Rightarrow (1-u)f(v)=(1-v)f(u)$. But $1-x$ is invertible in $\mathcal{D}(G)$ for all $x\neq 1$, so $(1-v)^{-1}f(v)=(1-u)^{-1}f(u)$.
	
	If $uvu=v$ then $f(uvu)=f(v)\Rightarrow f(u)+uf(v)+uvf(u)=f(v)\Rightarrow (1+uv)f(u)=(1-u)f(v)$. Observe that $(1+uv)(1-u)=(1-u)(1-v)$ and so $(1-u)(1-v)(1-u)^{-1}f(u)=(1-u)f(v)\Rightarrow (1-v)^{-1}f(v)=(1-u)^{-1}f(u)$.

title: Remark
body_md:
Let $A_\Gamma$ be an Artin group that is torsion-free and satisfies the Atiyah conjecture. Let $f\in \operatorname{Der}(A_\Gamma,\mathcal{D}(A_\Gamma))$. Every canonical relator has the form $$\langle u,v\rangle_n=\langle v,u\rangle_n$$ for some $n$, where $\langle u,v\rangle_n=\underbrace{uvuv\cdots}_{n\text{ letters}}$. If $n$ is even, applying $f$ to the relator and using the derivation rule gives
	$$\bigl(1-v+uv-vuv+\cdots-\langle v,u\rangle_{n-1}\bigr)f(u)=\bigl(1-u+vu-uvu+\cdots-\langle u,v\rangle_{n-1}\bigr)f(v).$$
	
	Moreover, $(1-v+uv-vuv+\cdots-\langle v,u\rangle_{n-1})(1-u)=(1-u+vu-uvu+\cdots-\langle u,v\rangle_{n-1})(1-v)$. These two identities imply $(1-v)^{-1}f(v)=(1-u)^{-1}f(u)$. In the case where $n$ is odd we can similarly prove that $(1-v)^{-1}f(v)=(1-u)^{-1}f(u)$.
	
	Hence, if $A_\Gamma$ is torsion-free and satisfies the Atiyah conjecture, a similar argument as in the twisteed RAAG case shows that $\beta_1^{(2)}(A_\Gamma)=\overline{\beta}_0(\Gamma)$. This is also a particular case of Davis-Leary theorem for $n=1$ (see Theorem \ref{BettiRAAG}). Some families of torsion-free Artin groups satisfying the Atiyah conjecture are RAAGs, even Artin groups of FC-type \cite{Blasco-Martinez} and even Artin groups of large type \cite{Blasco}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $v_{i_1,i_2}$ and $v_{i_1+1,i_2}$ lie in the same connected component of $\Delta$, Lemma~\ref{Derivation Lemma}.1 gives
	$$(1-v_{i_1,i_2})^{-1}f(v_{i_1,i_2})=(1-v_{i_1+1,i_2})^{-1}f(v_{i_1+1,i_2})\Rightarrow
	f(v_{i_1+1,i_2})=(1-v_{i_1+1,i_2})(1-v_{i_1,i_2})^{-1}f(v_{i_1,i_2}).$$

	On the other hand, the relation $v_{i_1,i_2}=v_{i_1+1,i_2}^{X_{i_1,i_2}}$
	gives
	$$f(v_{i_1,i_2}X_{i_1,i_2})=f(X_{i_1,i_2}v_{i_1+1,i_2})\Rightarrow f(v_{i_1,i_2})+v_{i_1,i_2}f(X_{i_1,i_2})=f(X_{i_1,i_2})+X_{i_1,i_2}f(v_{i_1+1,i_2}).$$
	Substituting the expression for $f(v_{i_1+1,i_2})$ obtained above and rearranging, we obtain
	$$(1-v_{i_1,i_2})f(X_{i_1,i_2})=f(v_{i_1,i_2})+X_{i_1,i_2}(1-v_{i_1+1,i_2})(1-v_{i_1,i_2})^{-1}f(v_{i_1,i_2}).$$
	
	Since $X_{i_1,i_2}=(1-v_{i_1,i_2})X_{i_1,i_2}(1-v_{i_1+1,i_2})^{-1},$ we have
	$$(1-v_{i_1,i_2})f(X_{i_1,i_2})=f(v_{i_1,i_2})+(1-v_{i_1,i_2})X_{i_1,i_2}(1-v_{i_1,i_2})^{-1}f(v_{i_1,i_2}).$$
	Rearranging gives $(1-X_{i_1,i_2})^{-1}f(X_{i_1,i_2})=(1-v_{i_1,i_2})^{-1}f(v_{i_1,i_2})$, as required.	
	
	Since $u_1$ and $u_2$ lie in the same connected component of $\Gamma$ there is at least one connected component of Type $4$. Let $v_{i_1,i_2},w_{i_3,i_4}$ be two vertices in $\Delta$ such that $v$ and $w$ lie in Type $4$ connected components of $\Gamma$. If $v$ and $w$ lie in the same connected component of $\Gamma_{u_1,u_2}$ then $v_{i_1,i_2}$ and $w_{i_3,i_4}$ lie in the same connected component of $\Delta$, so by  Lemma~\ref{Derivation Lemma}.1 $(1-v_{i_1,i_2})^{-1}f(v_{i_1,i_2})=(1-w_{i_3,i_4})^{-1}f(w_{i_3,i_4})$. $v$ and $w$ lie in distinct connected component of $\Gamma_{u_1,u_2}$ then by the above discussion $(1-v_{i_1,i_2})^{-1}f(v_{i_1,i_2})=(1-X_{i_5,i_6})^{-1}f(X_{i_5,i_6})=(1-w_{i_3,i_4})^{-1}f(w_{i_3,i_4})$ for any $0<i_5<o(u_1)$ and  $0<i_6<o(u_2)$. Hence $(1-a)^{-1}f(a)$ is a constant value on the following set:
	 $$\lbrace v_{i_1,i_2}\mid 	0\leq i_k<o(u_k)\text{ with }k=1,2\text{ and }v\text{ is of Type }4\rbrace \cup\lbrace X_{i_1,i_2}\mid 	0<i_k<o(u_k)\text{ with }k=1,2\rbrace $$
	 Hence this set of generators contribute to $1$ dimension to $\mathrm{Der}\bigl(\ker(\varphi),\mathcal{D}(\ker(\varphi))\bigr)$.

title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\Omega$ be a connected component of Type $2$, and let
	$v\in V(\Omega)\cap\operatorname{lk}(u_1)$. Then $v_{i_1,i_2}X_{i_1,i_2}=X_{i_1,i_2}v_{i_1+1,i_2}$ for $0\leq i_k<o(u_k)$, $k=1,2$. If $f\in\mathrm{Der}\bigl(\ker(\varphi),\mathcal{D}(\ker(\varphi))\bigr)$, then
	$$f(v_{i_1,i_2})+v_{i_1,i_2}f(X_{i_1,i_2})=f(X_{i_1,i_2})+X_{i_1,i_2}f(v_{i_1+1,i_2}).$$
	Thus, the value $f(v_{i_1+1,i_2})$ is completely determined by
	$f(X_{i_1,i_2})$ and $f(v_{i_1,i_2})$. By Proposition~\ref{Type4}, the value of $f(X_{i_1,i_2})$ is completely determined by the Type $4$ connected components. Hence, for each fixed $i_2$, the value $f(v_{0,i_2})$ determines the values
	$f(v_{i_1,i_2})$ for all
	$i_1\in{1,\dots,o(u_1)-1}$.
	Therefore, all vertices of $\Delta$ arising from $\Omega$ are determined by the values
	$f(v_{0,i_2})$ for
	$i_2\in{0,\dots,o(u_2)-1}$.
	Thus, each Type $2$ connected component contributes $o(u_2)$ dimensions to
	$\mathrm{Der}\bigl(\ker(\varphi),\mathcal{D}(\ker(\varphi))\bigr)$.
	Since the number of Type $2$ connected components is
	$\beta_1^{(2)}(A_{\Gamma_{u_1}})
	-\beta_1^{(2)}(A_\Gamma)$, the claimed contribution follows.

title: Theorem
body_md:
Let $\mathcal{G}_\Gamma$ be a graph product of cyclic groups with
	$V(\Gamma^{\infty})={u,v}$, and assume that $u$ and $v$ are not adjacent. Then
	$$\beta_1^{(2)}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)=\left(1-\frac{1}{o(u)}-\frac{1}{o(v)}\right)\beta_1^{(2)}(A_\Gamma)+\frac{1}{o(u)}\beta_1^{(2)}(A_{\Gamma_u})+\frac{1}{o(v)}\beta_1^{(2)}(A_{\Gamma_v}).$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First suppose that $u$ and $v$ lie in the same connected component of $\Gamma$. Then the result follows by adding the contributions to the dimension of
	$\mathrm{Der}\bigl(\ker(\varphi),\mathcal{D}(\ker(\varphi))\bigr)$
	from the four types of connected components described in Lemmas~\ref{Type 1}, \ref{Type 2}, \ref{Type 3}, and Proposition~\ref{Type4}. Now suppose that $u$ and $v$ lie in different connected components. We can then write $\mathcal{G}_\Gamma=\mathcal{G}_{\Gamma^1}\ast\mathcal{G}_{\Gamma^2}$, where $u\in V(\Gamma^1)$ and $v\in V(\Gamma^2)$. Assume that $\lvert V(\Gamma^1)\rvert,\lvert V(\Gamma^2)\rvert>1$, since the other two cases follow similarly. By \cite[Theorem 4.15(ii)]{Kammeyer},
	$$
	\beta_1^{(2)}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)=\beta_1^{(2)}(\mathcal{G}_{\Gamma^1})+\beta_1^{(2)}(\mathcal{G}_{\Gamma^2})+1.$$
	By Theorem~\ref{BettiClique}, we have
	$$\beta_1^{(2)}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)
		=\frac{1}{o(u)}\left((o(u)-1)\beta_1^{(2)}(A_{\Gamma^1})+\beta_1^{(2)}(A_{\Gamma^1_u})\right)+\frac{1}{o(v)}\left((o(v)-1)\beta_1^{(2)}(A_{\Gamma^2})+\beta_1^{(2)}(A_{\Gamma^2_v})\right)+1.
	$$
	On the other hand, since the first $\ell^2$-Betti number of a RAAG is given by the number of connected components of its defining graph minus $1$, we have
	$$
	\beta_1^{(2)}(A_\Gamma)
	=
	\beta_1^{(2)}(A_{\Gamma^1})
	+
	\beta_1^{(2)}(A_{\Gamma^2})
	+
	1,
	$$
	$$
	\beta_1^{(2)}(A_{\Gamma_u})
	=
	\beta_1^{(2)}(A_{\Gamma^1_u})
	+
	\beta_1^{(2)}(A_{\Gamma^2})
	+
	1,
	$$
	and
	$$
	\beta_1^{(2)}(A_{\Gamma_v})
	=
	\beta_1^{(2)}(A_{\Gamma^1})
	+
	\beta_1^{(2)}(A_{\Gamma^2_v})
	+
	1.
	$$
	Substituting these identities into the preceding expression for
	$\beta_1^{(2)}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$ yields the desired formula.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $u$ and $v$ are adjacent, the result follows from Theorem~\ref{BettiClique}. Suppose now that $u$ and $v$ are not adjacent. A direct count of the connected components yields
	$$\beta_1^{(2)}(A_{\Gamma_{uv}})=\beta_1^{(2)}(A_{\Gamma_u})+\beta_1^{(2)}(A_{\Gamma_v})-\beta_1^{(2)}(A_\Gamma).$$
	Combining this identity with the formula from the previous theorem, we obtain the desired formula.

title: Remark
body_md:
In the setting of the above theorem, suppose in addition that $\mathcal{G}_\Gamma$ is two-dimensional, that is, that $\Gamma$ contains no triangles. Then $\beta_i^{(2)}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)=0$ for all $i\geq 3$, and hence the second $\ell^2$-Betti number can be determined from the Euler characteristic. By \cite{Chriswell}, if $\deg(w)$ counts the number of vertices that are adjacent to $w$ in $\Gamma$: $$\chi(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)=1-\lvert V(\Gamma)\rvert+\lvert E(\Gamma)\rvert+\frac{1-\deg(u)}{o(u)}+\frac{1-\deg(v)}{o(v)}.$$
	Consequently, $\beta_2^{(2)}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)=\beta_1^{(2)}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)+\chi(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$.
	 As a concrete example, if $\Gamma$ is a cycle with $n$ vertices, then
	$$\beta_i^{(2)}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)
	=
	\begin{dcases}
		1-\dfrac{1}{o(u)}-\dfrac{1}{o(v)}, & \text{if } i=2,\\[6pt]
		0, & \text{otherwise}.
	\end{dcases}$$

label: Sigma1
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Sigma1}
	Let $\mathcal{G}_\Gamma$ be a graph product of cyclic groups. Then
	\[
	\Sigma^1(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)=\{[\chi]\in S(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)\mid\mathrm{Liv}^\chi\text{ is connected and dominant}\}.
	\]
	A subgraph $\Gamma'\subset\Gamma$ is called \textbf{dominant} if, for every vertex $v\in V(\Gamma\setminus\Gamma')$, there exists a vertex $w\in V(\Gamma')$ such that $\{v,w\}\in E(\Gamma)$.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{DeligneLemma}
	Let $S=\mathcal{G}_\Delta$ be a graph product of cyclic groups based on a complete graph $\Delta$ with $\left|V(\Delta)\right|=s\neq0$. Then, $\mathrm{Del}^S$ is homotopically equivalent to a wedge of $(s-1)$-spheres, so it is $(s-2)$-connected.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: For each $v\in V(\Delta)$ and $g\in S$ let $gX_v$ be the subcomplex of $\mathrm{Del}^S$ induced by $\lbrace g\mathcal{G}_\Omega\mid\Omega\subset\Delta_v\rbrace$. The set $\lbrace gX_v\mid g\in S,v\in V(\Delta)\rbrace$ is a covering of $\mathrm{Del}^S$. One can see that any set of pairwise distinct $g_0X_{v_0},\dots, g_k X_{v_k}$ has empty intersection if two of the $v_i's$ are equal and that whenever such a set has a non-empty intersection the intersection of a subcomplex with a maximal element, hence it is contractible. Thus, $\mathrm{Del}^S$ is homotopy equivalent to the nerve of the covering (cf. \cite{Brown 2012} Chapter VII Theorem 4.4) and by (cf. \cite{Deligne 1972} Theorem 2.15) this complex is a wedge of $(s-1)$-spheres.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let us prove the homological one first. We first need to prove that $C(\mathcal{H})$ is $(n-1)$-acyclic for which we use Lemma \ref{Conectivity Lemma}. $C(\mathcal{P})$ is contractible by \cite{Davis 1998} and $\mathrm{Del}^S$ is $(s-2)$-connected by Lemma \ref{DeligneLemma}, so we just need to prove that $\left|\mathcal{J}_S\right|$ is $(n-s-1)$-connected for each $S=\mathcal{G}_\Delta\in\mathcal{P}\setminus\mathcal{H}$ and with $\left|V(S)\right|=s$. Let $\mathcal{L}^\chi_\Delta$ be the poset of simplices of $\widehat{\mathrm{lk}_{\mathrm{Liv}^\chi}(\Delta)}$ and define the map:
	$$\begin{aligned}
		\tau :\mathcal{L}^\chi_\Delta & \longrightarrow \mathcal{J}_S \\
		Y & \longmapsto Y\cup\Delta
	\end{aligned}$$
	one sees that for each $X\in\mathcal{J}_S$ $\tau^{-1}_{\leq}(X)=\lbrace Y\in \mathcal{L}^\chi_\Delta\mid Y\cup\Delta\subset X\rbrace$ which has $X\setminus\Delta$ as a maximal element, thus it is contractible. Then, by Quillen's Lemma (cf. \cite{Benson} Lemma 6.5.2) $\tau$ induces an homotopy equivalence between the geometric realizations. Hence, the homological $n$-link conditions imply that $\left|\mathcal{L}^\chi_\Delta\right|$, and so $\left|\mathcal{J}_S\right|$ is $(n-s-1)$-acyclic. Hence $C(\mathcal{H})$ is an $(n-1)$-acyclic space with stabilizers of the form $g\mathcal{G}_\Delta g^{-1}$ with $g\in\mathcal{G}_\Gamma$ and $\mathcal{G}_\Delta\in\mathcal{H}$. Applying Theorem \ref{teo:MMVW} the claim follows. The same proof works for the homotopical case.

label: FiniteAut
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{FiniteAut}
Let $\mathcal{G}_\Gamma$ be a graph product of cyclic groups. Then $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$ is finite if and only if $\Gamma$ is complete and $|V(\Gamma^\infty)|\leq 1$, where $V(\Gamma^\infty)$ denotes the set of vertices corresponding to infinite cyclic vertex groups.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$ is finite, then its subgroup of inner automorphisms
$\mathrm{Inn}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)=\mathcal{G}_\Gamma/\mathrm{Z}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$
is also finite.
We know that $\mathcal{G}_\Gamma/\mathrm{Z}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)\cong \mathcal{G}_\Delta$, where $\Delta$ is the subgraph induced by the vertices $v\in V(\Gamma)$ with $\mathrm{st}(v)\neq \Gamma$.
If this quotient is finite, then $\Delta$ must be complete, which implies $\mathrm{st}(v)=\Gamma$ for all $v\in V(\Gamma)$. Hence, if $\mathcal{G}_\Gamma/\mathrm{Z}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$ is finite then $\mathcal{G}_\Gamma=\mathrm{Z}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$, i.e. $\Gamma$ is complete.

In this case, $\mathcal{G}_\Gamma\cong \mathbb{Z}^k\times G$, where $G$ is a finite group.
If $k=0$, then $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$ is clearly finite. Suppose $k>0$. Then $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{Z}^k)$ embeds as a finite-index subgroup of $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{Z}^k\times G)$. Thus $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$ is finite if and only if $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{Z}^k)$ is finite, which occurs precisely when $k=1$. This proves the claim.

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $\Gamma$ be a simplicial graph and $u,v\in V(\Gamma)$ be non-adjacent vertices.
The pair $(u,v)$ forms a \textbf{separating intersection of links (SIL)} if there exists a connected component of $\Gamma\setminus(\mathrm{lk}(u)\cap\mathrm{lk}(v))$ which contains neither $u$ nor $v$.

label: Finite index Torelli
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{Finite index Torelli}
Let $\mathcal{G}_\Gamma$ be a graph product of cyclic groups such that whenever 
$\mathrm{lk}(u)\subset \mathrm{st}(v)$ and $o(u)=\infty$, we have $o(v)<\infty$. 
Then $\mathrm{IA}_\Gamma$ has finite index in $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\mathrm{Aut}^1_\infty(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$ denote the subgroup of $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$ generated by all partial conjugations and by those transvections $\tau^v_u$ with $u,v\in V(\Gamma)$ satisfying $\mathrm{lk}(u)\subset \mathrm{st}(v)$ and $o(u)=\infty$. 
By \cite[Corollary 2.8]{Sale-Susse}, this subgroup has finite index in $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$ and contains $\mathrm{IA}_\Gamma$.

Under the given hypothesis, no transvection of infinite order occurs. 
Hence, by \cite[Lemma 5.3]{Sale-Susse}, the image $\rho(\mathrm{Aut}^1_\infty(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma))$ in $\mathrm{Aut}(\overline{\mathcal{G}}_\Gamma)$ is finite. 
Since $\mathrm{IA}_\Gamma=\ker(\rho|_{\mathrm{Aut}^1_\infty(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)})$, it follows that $\mathrm{IA}_\Gamma$ is of finite index in $\mathrm{Aut}^1_\infty(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$, and consequently of finite index in $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$.

label: FiniteOut
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If any of these conditions fails, then $\mathrm{Out}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$ is infinite.
Indeed, if $(u,v)$ is a SIL and $C_u,C_v$ denote the connected components of $\Gamma\setminus\mathrm{st}(u)$ and $\Gamma\setminus\mathrm{st}(v)$ containing $v$ and $u$ respectively, then $\pi_{C_u}^u\pi_{C_v}^v$ has infinite order (c.f. \cite[Section 4]
{Gutierrez-Piggott-Ruane}).
Similarly, violation of conditions (2) or (3) produces standard generators of infinite order.

Conversely, assume that all three conditions hold.
By Proposition~\ref{Finite index Torelli}, $\mathrm{IA}_\Gamma$ has finite index in $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$.
Since $\Gamma$ has no SILs, it follows from \cite[Section 4]
{Gutierrez-Piggott-Ruane} that all partial conjugations commute.
Hence $\mathrm{IA}_\Gamma$ is a finite abelian group.
Therefore, $\mathrm{Out}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$ contains a finite subgroup of finite index, and is itself finite.

label: LemmaDisconnected
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{LemmaDisconnected}
	Let $\mathcal{G}_\Gamma$ be a graph product of cyclic groups with $\operatorname{Out}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$ finite. Assume that $\Gamma$ is connected and that there exists $v\in V(\Gamma)$ such that $o(v)<\infty$ and $\Gamma_v$ is disconnected. If there exists a connected component $C$ of $\Gamma_v$ lying entirely in $\Gamma^\infty$, then $\left|V(C)\right|=1$ and $\Gamma_v$ has two connected component.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Let $w\in V(C)$ be a vertex adjacent to $v$. Since $\operatorname{Out}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$ is finite, the graph $\Gamma\setminus\operatorname{st}(w)$ is connected. Hence, $C=\operatorname{st}(w)\setminus\{v\}$, and the same holds for every $w\in V(C)$. Therefore, for every $u,w\in V(C)$ we have $\operatorname{lk}(u)\subseteq\operatorname{st}(w)$. This implies that  $\left|V(C)\right|=1$, otherwise $\operatorname{Out}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$ would be infinite. It also follows that $\Gamma_v$ splits in two connected components $C$ and $\Gamma\setminus(C\cup\lbrace v\rbrace)$.

label: Gamma connected
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For the first statement, suppose by contradiction that $\Gamma$ is disconnected. 
By \cite[Lemma~2.17]{Escartin}, since $\Gamma$ has no SILs, it must be the disjoint union of two complete subgraphs. 
The only such configuration with no infinite-order transvections corresponds to a disconnected graph with two vertices, and hence $\mathcal{G}_\Gamma \cong \mathbb{Z}\ast \mathbb{Z}/o(v)\mathbb{Z}$.

For the second statement, assume that $\Gamma_v$ is disconnected, with connected components $\Gamma_1,\dots,\Gamma_n$. By 1. $\Gamma$ is connected, so we can use Lemma \ref{LemmaDisconnected} and it follows that $\left|V(\Gamma_1)\right|=\dots=\left|V(\Gamma_n)\right|=1$. Therefore
$$\mathcal{G}_\Gamma \cong F_n\times \mathbb{Z}/o(v)\mathbb{Z},$$
which admits transvections of infinite order unless $n=1$. Hence, since  $\mathrm{Out}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$ is finite it follows that $n=1$ and $\mathcal{G}_\Gamma \cong \mathbb{Z}\times \mathbb{Z}/o(v)\mathbb{Z}$, contradicting that $\Gamma_v$ is disconnected.

title: Proof
body_md:
(Theorem \ref{Main4})
By Proposition~\ref{FiniteAut}, the group $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$ is finite if and only if $\Gamma$ is a complete graph on one or two vertices. 
Hence we may assume that we are not in these cases.

Consider the short exact sequence
$$1 \longrightarrow \mathcal{G}_\Gamma/\mathrm{Z}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)
\longrightarrow \mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)
\longrightarrow \mathrm{Out}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)
\longrightarrow 1.$$
If $\mathcal{G}_\Gamma/\mathrm{Z}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$ is finite, then $\mathcal{G}_\Gamma=\mathrm{Z}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$, so 
$\mathcal{G}_\Gamma \cong \mathbb{Z}^k\times  \mathbb{Z}/o(v)\mathbb{Z}$. 
In this case $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{Z}^k)$ embeds as a finite-index subgroup of $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{Z}^k\times  \mathbb{Z}/o(v)\mathbb{Z})$, and 
$\beta_1^{(2)}(\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{Z}^k))\neq 0$ if and only if $k=2$.

If both $\mathcal{G}_\Gamma/\mathrm{Z}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$ and $\mathrm{Out}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$ are infinite, then by \cite[Theorem~7.2~(7)]{Luck} we have $\beta_1^{(2)}(\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma))=0$. 
Therefore, we may assume that $\mathrm{Out}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$ is finite, so that $\mathcal{G}_\Gamma/\mathrm{Z}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$ has finite index in $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$.

If $\mathrm{Z}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)\neq 1$, then $\mathrm{Z}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)=\langle v\rangle$; otherwise, by condition~(3) of Proposition~\ref{FiniteOut}, $\mathrm{Out}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$ would be infinite. 
In this case $\mathcal{G}_\Gamma/\mathrm{Z}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)\cong A_{\Gamma_v}$, which is a right-angled Artin group. 
By Lemma~\ref{Gamma connected}(2), the graph $\Gamma_v$ is connected, so $\beta_1^{(2)}(A_{\Gamma_v})=0$, and hence $\beta_1^{(2)}(\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma))=0$.

If $\mathrm{Z}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)=1$, then $\mathcal{G}_\Gamma$ has finite index in $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$. 
By Theorem~\ref{BettiClique}, $\beta_1^{(2)}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)=0$ if and only if both $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma_v$ are connected. 
Thus, by Lemma~\ref{Gamma connected}, we deduce that $\beta_1^{(2)}(\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma))=0$ unless $\mathcal{G}_\Gamma\cong\mathbb{Z}\ast\mathbb{Z}/o(v)\mathbb{Z}$, completing the proof.

title: Definition
body_md: Assume $\mathcal{G}_\Gamma$ is a graph product  of cyclic groups with $V(\Gamma^{<\infty})=\{u,v\}$ that $\Gamma,\Gamma_u,\Gamma_v$ are connected and that $\Gamma_{u,v}$ is disconnected. If the decomposition of $\Gamma_{u,v}$ in connected components is $C_1\sqcup\dots\sqcup C_n$ we say that $\Gamma$ is of \textbf{type $\mathcal{P}$} if at most one connected component $C_i$ satisfies $V(C_i)=1$ and every other component $C_j$ satisfies that the only infinite order generators of $\operatorname{Out}(A_{C_j\cup\{u,v\}})$, if any, are partial conjugations or transvections with respect to $u$ and $v$.

title: Proof
body_md:
For the first statement, suppose by contradiction that $\Gamma$ is disconnected. By \cite[Lemma~2.17]{Escartin}, since $\Gamma$ has no SILs, it must be the disjoint union of two complete subgraphs. Since there cannot be infinite-order transvections there are at most one infinite labelled vertex in each connected components, thus it easily follows that $\mathcal{G}_\Gamma$ is either $\mathbb{Z}\ast\left(\mathbb{Z}/o(u)\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/o(v)\mathbb{Z}\right)$ or $\left(\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/o(u)\mathbb{Z}\right)\ast\left(\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/o(v)\mathbb{Z}\right)$.
	
	For $2.$,  by Lemma \ref{LemmaDisconnected} it follows that $\Gamma_v$ splits in two connected components, one containing $u$ and one having just one vertex. Call $C$ the component of $u$. There are two situations, let us first assume that there exists $u\neq w\in V(C)$ with $\{v,w\}\in E(\Gamma)$. Then $C=\operatorname{st}(w)\setminus\{v\}$. Hence $\operatorname{lk}(r)\subset\operatorname{st}(w)$ for each $r\in V(C)$. Since $\mathrm{Out}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$ is finite that implies that $V(C)=\lbrace w,u\rbrace$. This lead us to two possible graphs, depending on whether $\lbrace u,w\rbrace\in E(\Gamma)$ or not. Now assume that there is no $u\neq w\in V(C)$ with $\{v,w\}\in E(\Gamma)$, so $\operatorname{lk}(v)\cap C=\{u\}$. We have two possibilities, if $\Gamma_u$ is connected then $V(C)=\{u\}$, and if $\Gamma_u$ is disconnected, by Lemma \ref{LemmaDisconnected}  we have  $\left|V(C)\right|=2$. Hence, each case gives one of the four graphs of the statement.
	
	For the last statement assume that the decomposition of $\Gamma_{u,v}$ in connected components is $C_1\sqcup\dots\sqcup C_n$.  For each connected component $C_i$ we have two cases:
	\begin{itemize}
		\item If there exists $w\in V(C_i)$ such that $\{w,v\},\{w,u\}\in E(\Gamma)$ then, arguing as in Lemma \ref{LemmaDisconnected} it follows that $C_i=\{w\}$. Moreover, if there are two connected components $C_i=\{w\}$ and $C_j=\{r\}$ it follows that $\operatorname{lk}(w)\subset\operatorname{st}(r)$ contradicting that $\operatorname{Out}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$ is finite. Hence there can only be one connected component with one vertex.
		\item If there is no $w\in V(C_i)$ as above then $\left|V(C_i)\right|>1$, otherwise either $\Gamma_u$ or $\Gamma_v$ would be disconnected. Since $\operatorname{Out}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$ is finite it follows that all partial conjugations and transvections, if any, are with respect to $u$ or $v$.
	\end{itemize}
	Therefore $\Gamma$ is a type $\mathcal{P}$ graph. By way of contradiction assume that $\mathrm{Z}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)\neq1$. Since $\{u,v\}$ disconnects $\Gamma$ that means that either $u\in\mathrm{Z}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$ or $v\in\mathrm{Z}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$. If $u\in\mathrm{Z}(\mathcal{G}_\Gamma)$ then $\operatorname{st}(u)=\Gamma$. Let $w\in V(C_i)$ and assume that $\left|V(C_i)\right|>1$, then $\{v,w\}\notin E(\Gamma)$. This implies that $C_i$ is a connected component of $\Gamma_u$, which is a contradiction.
